rv.q: Yet with Cox on full song, The Score is always interesting, even when it’s not convincing.
The Score is solid enough commercial entertainment, but really it's a second tier show built around one top tier cast member.
The dramatic arrangement of the challenge is very craftily handled with plenty of surprises to keep you guessing.
The Score, which comes to the West End after premièring in Bath two years ago, misses something, but its production and performances make it worth seeing.
Cox’s impassioned, emotionally wrought portrayal of fading genius that shines brightest.
But though The Score occasionally flares enjoyably to life, as we enter Lent season you’d be better off seeking out one of the many Bach Passion performances to get a sense of the man it depicts.
Not the best publicity in the run-up to the opening of a fairly boring play in the West End.
On the whole, The Score scores highly on all fronts.
Feeling like a work in progress but one that is far from finished, The Score has plenty of potential but is not the best version of itself as yet.
There’s very little praise to spare for The Score, which mournfully plays against its title.

cn.t: Brian Cox's magnetic performance elevates this historical drama about Bach's meeting with Frederick the Great, though critics find the play itself only moderately successful at capturing the composer's genius.
